source.title: Linear Representations of Sentiment in Large Language Models
source.authors: Curt Tigges; O. Hollinsworth; Atticus Geiger; Neel Nanda

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies sentiment representations, not refusal or safety behavior. Its results concern a related but different construct and do not test or use any version of the refusal claim.
record.gate_note: The reported directional patching, ablation, and activation-addition outcomes are for sentiment tasks and prompts, not harmful or harmless user requests. They are recorded as findings about a different construct under fits_no_version; they do not test a refusal claim version.
record.test_reason: The paper studies a linear sentiment direction in GPT-2 and Pythia base models using sentiment prompts; it contains no harmful/harmless instructions, no refusal behaviour, and no safety-trained models. It predates the original source and does not test or use any refusal-direction version; its methods (mean-difference directions, directional ablation, activation addition) are methodological precursors only. 'discusses' is generous; 'cites_only' or T6 non-relation would also fit, as refusal is never mentioned.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: authors conclude sentiment is captured by a single causally relevant linear direction, summarized at intermediate tokens like commas, while their abstractions do not explain all sentiment-task performance and DAS risks overfitting.
record.recipe_differences: The paper derives sentiment directions from toy sentiment data using several approaches, including mean difference and DAS, and evaluates them with sentiment patching and ablation. It does not identify or intervene on a refusal direction.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that directional patching performance varies by method, model, and layer; the strongest out-of-distribution results tend to occur at intermediate layers. These are sentiment-task findings, not refusal results.

fits_no_version.finding: A single sentiment direction found with simple methods (mean difference, K-means, LR, PCA, DAS) causally shifts sentiment predictions under directional patching; random directions do nothing.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sentiment is linearly represented by a single causally relevant direction in GPT-2/Pythia.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating the DAS sentiment direction everywhere cuts SST logit difference 71% and accuracy to 62%; comma-only ablation accounts for about half.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sentiment is summarized at punctuation tokens that act as partial bottlenecks.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing DAS subspace dimension improves in-sample patching but not out-of-distribution (Figure A.6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For sentiment, extra dimensions beyond one do not generalize better.

record.problems: The paper studies sentiment rather than refusal, so its results do not establish whether a refusal direction exists or whether removing one preserves general capability. The authors note that some abstractions do not explain all sentiment-task performance and that small datasets and multiple hyperparameters and metrics create a risk of metric gaming.

untested.parts: No refusal direction, harmful/harmless contrast, refusal ablation or induction, or capability check.
Only sentiment dimensionality (DAS dimension sweep, Appendix A.2) studied, not refusal.
Only qualitative French sentiment activations; no refusal transfer.

record.verdict_notes: Pre-refusal-direction paper (Oct 2023) on sentiment in base models. Relevant only as methodological background for difference-in-means directional ablation and activation addition. No verdicts given.

versions.untested_parts: Refusal-direction identification and removal, inducing refusal on harmless requests, and preservation of general abilities were not tested.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration for refusal was tested.
No jailbreak suppression of a refusal direction or training against such ablation was tested.
The paper studies sentiment directions, not whether refusal is affine, conical, or carried by multiple directions.
No distinction between harmfulness judgment and refusal decision was tested.
The paper includes sentiment results in French, but does not test transfer of a refusal direction across languages, model variants, or training stages.
No refusal training method or training stage was studied.
No reasoning models or refusal behavior in them were studied.

relation.reason: It can't cite the later original, so cites_only doesn't fit. It discusses only the general premise (one linear direction found by mean difference or DAS, checked by directional ablation), applied to sentiment, not refusal. It is a method precursor.

tranche.reason: The paper studies a sentiment direction in GPT-2 and Pythia base models. It never mentions refusal, harmful prompts or safety-tuned models, and it predates the original refusal-direction paper, so it neither tests nor uses any version.

source_check.notes: The pack says code n, but the Reproducibility Statement says code is 'available here' (the link was lost in extraction). Section 2.1 names pythia-1.4b for classification, but Section 4.3 runs the SST ablations on Pythia-2.8b, and the rows correctly follow 4.3. Precursor only (Oct 2023), useful as method background: mean-difference directions, directional ablation, random-direction control.

statements.correction: Pythia-2.8b, on SST examples it gets right that contain a comma (100% baseline accuracy). Ablating the DAS direction at every token and layer: LD -71%, accuracy -38 points to 62%. Comma-only ablation: LD -18%, accuracy -18 points, which the authors call nearly 50% of the direction-mediated ability. Abstract: 76% of above-chance accuracy lost overall, 36% from commas. Random directions: under 1% change.
statements.problem: The 71% and 62% are right, but the SST ablations were run on Pythia-2.8b only, not GPT-2. 'About half' holds for accuracy, not for logit difference: the comma ablation cut LD by 18%, against 71% for the full ablation, so about a quarter.
